outputs.evidence: Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment
outputs.answer: Searle's Chinese Room is a thought experiment in which a person who does not understand Chinese sits in a room with a rule book and, by following the rules, returns correct Chinese answers to Chinese questions passed in; from outside the room appears to understand Chinese, but nobody inside does [GAIF-1.3]. Searle's point is that manipulating symbols according to rules (syntax) is not the same as understanding meaning (semantics), so a program that behaves intelligently does not thereby have a mind — an argument against "strong AI", the idea that a suitably programmed computer literally has a mind [GAIF-1.3].

outputs.evidence: McCulloch-Pitts neuron
outputs.answer: A McCulloch-Pitts neuron fires when its net input exceeds a threshold, with equal excitatory weights and absolute inhibition, so with suitable weights and thresholds it can implement AND (weights 1 and 1, threshold 2) and OR (weights 2 and 2, threshold 2) [GAIF-2.5]. XOR, however, cannot be done by a single neuron; it needs a small two-layer network that combines "A and not B" with "not A and B" using inhibitory (negative) weights [GAIF-2.5].

outputs.evidence: define superintelligence
outputs.answer: Nick Bostrom (University of Oxford) defines superintelligence as any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all domains of interest. The pathways discussed are biological cognition (enhancing human brains), whole brain emulation (copying a brain in a computer) and artificial intelligence; when — or whether — this is possible is an open question. [GAIF-1.6]

outputs.evidence: vanishing gradient problem
outputs.answer:
The **vanishing gradient** problem arises because the sigmoid activation saturates: for very large positive or negative inputs its output flattens towards 1 or 0 and its derivative approaches 0. During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied layer by layer, so many small gradients multiply towards zero (0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 …), which is a major obstacle to training deep networks [GAIF-2.14].

**ReLU**, f(z) = max(0, z), helps because it does not saturate for positive inputs, is computationally very cheap (important for deep learning) and still introduces non-linearity [GAIF-2.14]. Glorot, Bordes and Bengio (2011) showed rectifier networks could be trained effectively and had advantages over sigmoid and tanh networks [GAIF-2.14].

outputs.evidence: prompt caching
outputs.answer: Prompt caching lets providers store the processed front of a context, so a later call starting with a byte-identical prefix is billed at a fraction of the normal input price and answers faster (on one provider, cache reads cost about 0.1× and writes 1.25–2×, with a minimum prefix length and a short default lifetime) [PEID-3.13]. The match is an exact prefix from the very start, so one changed character invalidates everything after it [PEID-3.13]. That is why a timestamp at the top of a system prompt silently disables caching: order the context stable first (tools, system prompt, examples) and volatile last (retrieved text, history, question) [PEID-3.13].

outputs.evidence: precision and recall
outputs.answer:
- **Precision** = TP/(TP+FP): of the ones we flagged, how many were right; its cost is wasted effort [PEID-5.6].
- **Recall** = TP/(TP+FN): of the ones that mattered, how many we caught; its cost is a missed case [PEID-5.6].
- **Accuracy** = (TP+TN)/all, and it lies on imbalanced data: a classifier that found three of four bug reports and raised six false alarms still scored 82.5% accuracy, because the large harmless true-negative box did the work [PEID-5.6].

outputs.evidence: workflow from an agent when building with LLMs
outputs.answer: The difference is who decides the next step, not intelligence. A **workflow** is a system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths written by a developer (e.g. classify → draft reply → send). An **agent** is a system where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use, choosing the next step at runtime (search, read a file, run tests, decide what next) [PEID-4.1].

outputs.evidence: raw agreement between annotators
outputs.answer: Cohen's kappa measures agreement between annotators after subtracting the agreement expected by chance: κ = (pₒ − pₑ)/(1 − pₑ), where pₒ is observed agreement and pₑ chance agreement; 1 is perfect and 0 means no better than chance [PEID-5.12]. Raw agreement flatters, because two annotators labelling a set that is 90% "other" can agree 90% of the time while guessing [PEID-5.12]. For example, observed 0.90 with chance 0.82 gives κ = 0.44, meaning the labels are barely usable [PEID-5.12].

outputs.evidence: how does attention decide which earlier words matter for the next token
outputs.answer: Attention re-weights all the tokens the model has already seen for every token it produces: in "the ticket the customer opened yesterday is still unresolved", the words "ticket" and "customer" get most of the weight and "the" almost none [PEID-1.4]. This weighting is learned, not programmed, and word order and position matter [PEID-1.4]. Before attention, models looked at a fixed window of nearby words and lost anything outside it; attention lets the model ask "which earlier word is this about?" at any distance [PEID-1.4].

outputs.evidence: why do people resist organisational change
outputs.answer:
Kotter and Schlesinger give four common reasons for resistance [DTGS-1.4]:

- **Parochial self-interest** — people focus on what they personally will lose rather than on the organisation as a whole [DTGS-1.4].
- **Misunderstanding and lack of trust** — they do not understand the change and its implications and do not trust those proposing it [DTGS-1.4].
- **Different assessments** — they evaluate the situation differently from the initiators and see more costs than benefits [DTGS-1.4].
- **Low tolerance for change** — fear of not being able to develop the new skills and behaviour required [DTGS-1.4].

outputs.evidence: cost per verified outcome
outputs.answer: Cost per verified outcome = (model + retrieval + verification + escalation + rework + governance cost) ÷ outcomes accepted by a human or a defined automatic test [DTGS-3.9]. It is tracked with four numbers: volume, containment, verification rate and defect escape rate [DTGS-3.9]. In the worked customer-service example (100,000 cases a month), the total is about €1.36, of which model inference is only €0.02 (1.5%), while escalation (€0.70) and rework (€0.33) dominate [DTGS-3.9].

outputs.evidence: Klarna's AI customer service assistant after its launch
outputs.answer: Klarna launched an AI assistant in February 2024 that handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, equated to about 700 full-time agents, cutting resolution time from 11 to under 2 minutes (company-reported claims) [DTGS-3.20]. In May 2025 its CEO said the focus on cost had led to lower quality; humans were reintroduced for disputes, fraud and hardship, with a commitment that customers can always reach a human, because satisfaction fell on complex and emotional cases even when answers were correct [DTGS-3.20]. By 2026 the framing settled: AI handles the simple tier and human service becomes almost a "VIP" premium tier — a business-model decision, not a technology one [DTGS-3.20].

outputs.evidence: Prosci's ADKAR model
outputs.answer: The letters in Prosci's ADKAR model stand for **Awareness**, **Desire**, **Knowledge**, **Ability** and **Reinforcement** [DTGS-1.7].

outputs.evidence: ground a model in its own documents with retrieval instead of fine-tuning
outputs.answer: Grounding with retrieval is the default when the model needs facts it cannot know: parametric memory is frozen at the training cut-off, contains nothing private, cannot be cited and can only be corrected by retraining, whereas non-parametric memory (an external store searched per question, with matching passages pasted into the window) is current, private, attributable and revocable [PEID-3.7]. RAG combines the two and is the default architecture of every "chat with your documents" product; the model does not learn your documents, it reads them once at the moment you ask [PEID-3.7]. No wording fixes a missing fact — putting the relevant clause in the window, delimiting it, requiring a verbatim quote and allowing "not covered by this policy" produces a correct, checkable answer [PEID-3.1]. Note also that prompting works on the finished model and cannot add knowledge, only steer behaviour that is already there [PEID-1.6].

outputs.evidence: judging the quality of a source
outputs.answer: The five source-quality checks are: **authority** (who produced it; are they qualified, accountable or directly involved?), **relevance** (does it answer your question or only a nearby one?), **timeliness** (is it recent enough for the topic?), **independence** (is it neutral, promotional, sponsored or selling something?) and **traceability** (can you see the evidence behind the claim?) [AITB-3.5].

outputs.evidence: when choosing an AI tool
outputs.answer: The tool-first trap is naming a tool ("we should use ChatGPT / Copilot / Zapier") before the task, data, risk, output and success criteria are clear [AITB-1.4]. Instead, state the work first — "we need to produce X for user Y, from approved data Z, with quality checks A and B" — and only then choose the category and the tool [AITB-1.4]. Tool selection should start with a bounded task: one narrow enough to test, review and improve [AITB-1.4].

outputs.evidence: business professional not use an AI tool
outputs.answer:
Do not use an AI tool when:

- The data is restricted (personal, confidential or client data without approval) [AITB-1.6].
- The decision is high-stakes (legal, medical, financial or employment) without qualified review [AITB-1.6].
- There is no verification path — outputs cannot be checked against sources, rules or calculations [AITB-1.6].
- There is a false-authority risk — the output will be consumed as official evidence without review [AITB-1.6].
- Ownership is unclear — nobody owns the prompt, data, output or consequences [AITB-1.6].

If the review step is impossible, the tool is probably not suitable yet [AITB-1.6].

outputs.evidence: AI-assisted research
outputs.answer: An evidence table is the control system of research: for every important claim it records the claim, source, date, exact evidence, whether it was verified, and notes (for example, an official feature launch page is verified, while a vendor blog claiming cost savings is promotional and needs independent evidence) [AITB-3.9]. Each claim follows the chain claim → source → evidence → check → limit, and the table should be built before writing the brief [AITB-3.9].

outputs.evidence: rather than have an AI draft it
outputs.answer: Write it yourself for condolences or bad news, disciplinary or performance letters, personal apologies, resignations or thanks, and anything read as personal — because authorship is the message, discovery damages trust, the words carry liability, nuance is the point and the time saved is trivial [AITB-4.10]. AI can still help check facts, dates and policy references or whether the tone will land [AITB-4.10]. If the reader would feel worse on learning it was generated, generate nothing [AITB-4.10].

outputs.evidence: hidden instructions
outputs.answer:
This is prompt injection: a document, email or web page given to the tool may contain instructions that try to redirect it, and that content is source content, not an authorised request [AITB-2.8].

To reduce it:
- Separate your instructions from source material and tell the tool to treat source text as data [AITB-2.8].
- Review unexpected changes of task or requests to share information [AITB-2.8].
- Limit connected permissions and require approval for consequential actions [AITB-2.8].
- Note that clear labels help, but prompt wording alone cannot reliably prevent prompt injection [AITB-2.8].

outputs.evidence: act as an expert
outputs.answer: No. A study of 162 roles across 2,410 questions (Zheng et al., 2024) found that adding personas to system prompts did not improve performance [PEID-2.6]. Role prompting reliably changes vocabulary and register, the default level of detail, what the answer leaves out, and format conventions, but it does not change factual accuracy, reasoning ability or competence the model never had [PEID-2.6]. It is a style control, not a competence control — say what you want done, not who you wish were doing it [PEID-2.6].

outputs.evidence: compare two versions of a prompt
outputs.answer:
To compare two prompt versions fairly, follow the prompt improvement loop: keep a baseline saved verbatim, collect 10–20 real inputs, read every failure and name it, change the one smallest thing that addresses the most common failure, then re-run the same inputs with the same settings and keep or revert [PEID-2.14]. Never change two things at once, never judge on one run, and keep the old version [PEID-2.14].

Because outputs are sampled, one run is not a measurement — quote either pass@k or pass^k and say which [PEID-5.1]. Use a frozen golden set of real, human-labelled inputs, never used in the prompt [PEID-5.10], and score with the cheapest grader that works [PEID-5.11].

outputs.evidence: ask an AI for a table or a fixed schema instead of free text
outputs.answer: A fixed schema (e.g. JSON with `category`, `urgency`, `evidence`) does three things: it collapses run-to-run variance, it turns the output into software (a parseable field can be routed, counted and stored), and it makes the output measurable — an `evidence` field also allows a cheap groundedness check [PEID-2.7]. The limit: a schema constrains the shape, never the truth; perfectly formed JSON can still hold the wrong category [PEID-2.7].

outputs.evidence: inventing facts that are not in the material I gave it
outputs.answer:
Supply the source material in the context and require a quoted evidence field, plus an escape hatch so abstention is allowed:

- Hallucination is the mechanism working as designed when the model is not grounded; the fix is to supply context, not to scold the model [PEID-1.9].
- No wording fixes a missing fact — put the relevant passage in the window, delimit it, require a verbatim quote and allow "not covered by this policy" [PEID-3.1].
- Symptom "it invents specifics": the fact is not in the context and the model always has a next token — supply the source, add an escape hatch, require a quoted evidence field [PEID-2.15].
- An `evidence` field in the output contract also allows a cheap groundedness check [PEID-2.7].
- Context-level fix: get the document in, require a quote, allow abstention [PEID-3.12].
- Always leave an escape hatch ("say *not stated*") or the model will fill the gap [PEID-2.4].

outputs.evidence: review and correct its own answer
outputs.answer:
Only under specific conditions. Intrinsic self-correction — a model reflecting on its own answer with no outside signal — often makes reasoning worse, because a model that got an answer wrong usually cannot tell [PEID-4.10]. Self-correction works when there is a reliable external check, such as passing tests, a retrieved fact or a verifier score [PEID-4.10].

An LLM judge can work, but only with four conditions together: a separate call (not the same turn reflecting on itself), a different prompt written to grade rather than answer, an external rubric with criteria the model did not invent while answering, and calibration against human labels [PEID-5.13]. Remove any one and you are back to self-correction [PEID-5.13].

outputs.evidence: why should a company worry about it
outputs.answer: Shadow AI is mentioned as a risk of the off-the-shelf tool rung of the make-or-buy ladder: low per-seat cost and low control come with a risk of shadow AI and data leakage [DTGS-3.7].

outputs.evidence: a company lets an AI answer its customers
outputs.answer:
Several risks are covered in the material:

- **Liability**: in *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024), a chatbot wrongly told a passenger he could claim a bereavement fare retroactively; the tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and held the company responsible for all information on its website — deflection transfers work, never liability [DTGS-3.21].
- **Trust cost and sensitive contexts**: trust collapses after one insensitive answer in sensitive contexts [DTGS-3.11].
- **Quality on complex and emotional cases**: Klarna reintroduced humans for disputes, fraud and hardship because satisfaction fell on complex and emotional cases even when answers were correct [DTGS-3.20].
- **Automation bias**: supervisors accept recommendations without adequate checking and miss errors they would have caught themselves, more so as the system becomes more reliable; if the override rate is under about 2%, the human in the loop is decorative [DTGS-3.21].
- **Model collapse**: AI-drafted notes entering CRMs and knowledge bases contaminate tomorrow's retrieval sources [DTGS-3.21].
- **Personalised pricing**: pricing the same good differently by inferred personal traits engages consumer law, GDPR and the AI Act in the EU [DTGS-3.21].
- **Unbounded rework tail**: removing verification saves €0.21 per case but opens an unbounded rework tail [DTGS-3.9].
- **A channel that can talk but not act** creates work rather than removing it [DTGS-3.11].
